title: How Organisations Learn, One Question at a Time
author: Andrea Chiarelli, Jason L Zimmerman
summary: Written with Jason Zimmerman, this piece argues that people without formal authority can still shift an organisation toward learning through the questions they ask. It traces a question through three acts: the private questions one asks oneself, the questions that enter a team conversation, and those that cross into steering groups and leadership reviews. At each level the authors name the conditions that let curiosity spread, such as safety to answer, simplicity, and leaders who thank rather than punish uncomfortable questions. They draw on a threshold model of collective behaviour to explain why repeated exposure tips norms. The closing section turns this into three Monday-morning moves: a private lens question, one question introduced into an existing conversation, and one question sent onward through a trusted relationship. The central claim is that culture change is the accumulation of small moments of asking rather than assuming.
points: A question first changes what its asker notices, so reframing frustration as a learning question is the starting point for any wider change.
For a question to catch on in a team it must be safe to answer, simple enough to repeat, and reliably useful each time it is used.
Leaders determine whether curiosity survives: defensive responses kill a question on contact, while thanking and acting on it signals that learning is wanted.
Incentives and information flow must reward early course-correction, or no one has reason to raise the uncomfortable question.
The practical path is three small moves: a private lens question, one question in a meeting you influence, and one question routed to a trusted person with wider reach.
quotes: Most companies say they want to be “learning organisations”. In practice, many of them run on a different fuel: directives, updates, and answers delivered as fast as possible. Work becomes a conveyor belt. Things move, but very little actually changes.
That is the first act of contagion: a question changes what one person pays attention to. Before it travels anywhere else, it rewires the experience of work for the person using it.
You haven’t criticised anyone. You haven’t derailed the agenda. You have simply placed a question in the middle of the table.

Of course, this can be shut down. If leaders respond defensively – “We don’t have time for philosophy, just get on with it” – the question dies on contact. If every meeting is packed so tightly that there’s no air for reflection, new habits can never take hold.
That is what it looks like when questions begin to operate at system level. They become part of the interface between strategy and reality.

Culture change often gets described in sweeping terms: new values, new strategies, new operating models. But under the hood, the day-to-day reality is far more granular: it is the accumulation of moments where someone decides to ask, rather than assume, to inquire, rather than instruct.
The goal isn’t to impress anyone, but to make it a little easier, and a little more normal, to talk about learning in the middle of the work.
